## Introduction

The calculation uses the linear growth factor $D(z)$, matter power spectrum
$P_m(k)$, filtered variance $\sigma^2(R)$, and multiplicity function to
evaluate $dn/d\ln M$ and halo counts per redshift.

## Prerequisites

Before running this example, make sure the `numcosmo_py`[^numcosmo_py] package is installed in your
environment. If it is not already installed, follow the [installation instructions in the NumCosmo documentation](https://numcosmo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html).
In addition, we are using `numpy` and `matplotlib` for data manipulation and plotting. If you are using
the [conda installation](https://numcosmo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html#mambaforge-development-environment),
these packages are already installed.

## Import and Initialize

First, import the required modules and initialize the NumCosmo library. The `Nc` and `Ncm` modules
provide the core functionality of the NumCosmo library. The call to `Ncm.cfg_init()` initializes the
library objects.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from numcosmo_py import Nc, Ncm

# Initialize the library
Ncm.cfg_init()
```

## Setting Up the Cosmological Model

We use a homogeneous and isotropic dark-energy model with a constant equation of state
(`NcHICosmoDEXcdm`). Rather than setting the dark-energy density directly, we switch to the curvature
parameterization with `omega_x2omega_k()` and fix `Omegak = 0.0`; flatness is then enforced as a
constraint and the dark-energy density is derived from the closure relation. A reionization model and a
power-law primordial power spectrum are built first and passed to the constructor: submodels are
construction-fixed and cannot be attached afterwards. We set the primordial amplitude and spectral
index explicitly: the amplitude fixes the normalization of the matter power spectrum, and through it
the overall scale of the mass function.

```{python}
# Reionization and a power-law primordial spectrum
reion = Nc.HIReionCamb.new()
prim = Nc.HIPrimPowerLaw.new()

# Set the primordial power spectrum parameters
prim["n_SA"] = 0.9658
prim["ln10e10ASA"] = 3.0904

# Dark-energy model with a constant equation of state. Submodels are
# construction-fixed: they must be passed here, not attached afterwards.
cosmo = Nc.HICosmoDEXcdm(reion=reion, prim=prim)

# Switch to the curvature parameterization and enforce flatness explicitly
cosmo.omega_x2omega_k()
cosmo["Omegak"] = 0.0

# Cosmological parameters. The list printed below is shorter than it may look:
# the primordial parameters set above (n_SA, ln10e10ASA) belong to prim, and Yp
# belongs to the nucleosynthesis submodel, so param_names() lists neither. The
# amplitude's effect shows up in the sigma8 print further down.
cosmo["H0"] = 70.0
cosmo["Omegab"] = 0.05
cosmo["Omegac"] = 0.25
cosmo["Tgamma0"] = 2.72
cosmo["w"] = -1.0

# Log all parameters
print("# Model parameters: ")
params = cosmo.param_names()

for param in params:
    print(f"{param} = {cosmo[param]}")
```

## Building the Mass-Function Ingredients

The halo mass function object is assembled from three pieces: a comoving-distance object, a
tophat-filtered linear power spectrum, and a multiplicity function. We build the linear power spectrum
from the Eisenstein-Hu transfer function, apply a tophat filter, and use the Tinker multiplicity
function with a mean overdensity of $\Delta = 200$. The filter is evaluated by an FFTLog transform from
$k$ to $r$, and `set_best_lnr0()` centres that transform on the $k$ range requested just above with
`require_kmin()`/`require_kmax()`, placing the radius range at the reciprocal of that range's centre and
carrying its logarithmic width across unchanged, so the filtered variance is defined over the scales
that $k$ range supports; `set_lnr0()` sets the range by hand instead.

```{python}
# Comoving-distance object, valid up to z = 2
dist = Nc.Distance.new(2.0)

# Eisenstein-Hu transfer function
tf = Nc.TransferFuncEH.new()

# Linear matter power spectrum built from the transfer function
psml = Nc.PowspecMLTransfer.new(tf)
psml.require_kmin(1.0e-3)
psml.require_kmax(1.0e3)

# Tophat-filtered variance, with the output interval tuned automatically
psf = Ncm.PowspecFilter.new(psml, Ncm.PowspecFilterType.TOPHAT)
psf.set_best_lnr0()

# Tinker multiplicity function, mean overdensity Delta = 200
mulf = Nc.MultiplicityFuncTinker.new()
mulf.set_mdef(Nc.MultiplicityFuncMassDef.MEAN)
mulf.set_Delta(200.0)

# Assemble the halo mass function
mf = Nc.HaloMassFunction.new(dist, psf, mulf)
```

## Growth Function

The linear growth factor $D(z)$ describes how density perturbations grow with time in the linear regime.
We obtain the growth-function object from the power spectrum, prepare it for the chosen cosmology, and
evaluate both $D(z)$ and its derivative over the redshift range $[0, 2]$.

```{python}
gf = psml.peek_gf()
gf.prepare(cosmo)

# Number of sampling points used throughout
n = 2000

z_a = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, n)
D_a = np.array([gf.eval(cosmo, z) for z in z_a])
dD_a = np.array([gf.eval_deriv(cosmo, z) for z in z_a])
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-hmf-growth
# | fig-cap: Linear growth function $D(z)$ and its derivative $dD/dz$.
# | fig-width: 100%
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(z_a, D_a, "r", label="$D(z)$")
plt.plot(z_a, dD_a, "b--", label="$dD/dz$")
plt.xlabel("$z$")
plt.title("Growth Function")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.show()
```

## Transfer Function and Matter Power Spectrum

Next we evaluate the Eisenstein-Hu transfer function $T(k)$ and the linear matter power spectrum
$P_m(k)$ at $z = 0$, over the wavenumber range $[10^{-3}, 10^{3}]\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$.

```{python}
psml.prepare(cosmo)

k_a = np.geomspace(1.0e-3, 1.0e3, n)
T_a = np.array([tf.eval(cosmo, k) for k in k_a])
Pm_a = np.array([psml.eval(cosmo, 0.0, k) for k in k_a])
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-hmf-transfer
# | fig-cap: >
# |   Eisenstein-Hu transfer function $T(k)$ and linear matter power spectrum $P_m(k)$
# |   at $z = 0$.
# | fig-width: 100%
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(k_a, T_a, "r", label="$T(k)$")
plt.plot(k_a, Pm_a, "b--", label="$P_m(k)$")
plt.xlabel(r"$k \; [\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}]$")
plt.xscale("log")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.title("Transfer Function and Linear Matter Power Spectrum")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.show()
```

## Filtered Variance

Applying the tophat filter, we compute the variance $\sigma^2(\ln R)$ of the density field smoothed on
scales $R \in [5, 50]\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ at $z = 0$, together with its logarithmic derivative
$d\ln\sigma^2 / d\ln R$. This logarithmic slope enters the mass function through the conversion between
mass and smoothing scale. We also print $\sigma_8$, the RMS density fluctuation on a scale of
$8\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, which is the number a mass-function normalization is usually read against;
`sigma8()` computes it directly from the filtered spectrum.

```{python}
psf.prepare(cosmo)

# Normalization benchmark: RMS fluctuation on 8 Mpc/h at z = 0
print(f"# sigma8 = {cosmo.sigma8(psf): .4f}")

R_a = np.geomspace(5.0, 50.0, n)
sigma2_a = np.array([psf.eval_var_lnr(0.0, np.log(R)) for R in R_a])
dlnsigma2_a = np.array([psf.eval_dlnvar_dlnr(0.0, np.log(R)) for R in R_a])
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-hmf-variance
# | fig-cap: >
# |   Tophat-filtered variance $\sigma^2(\ln R)$ and its logarithmic derivative at $z
# |   = 0$.
# | fig-width: 100%
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(R_a, sigma2_a, "r", label=r"$\sigma^2(\ln R)$")
plt.plot(R_a, dlnsigma2_a, "b--", label=r"$d\ln\sigma^2/d\ln R$")
plt.xlabel(r"$R \; [\mathrm{Mpc}]$")
plt.title("Variance and its Derivative")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.show()
```

## Halo Mass Function

With all ingredients in place, we set the survey solid angle (200 square degrees) and the integration
limits in mass and redshift, then prepare the mass function. We first evaluate the comoving number
density per logarithmic mass interval $dn / d\ln M$ at $z = 0.7$ over the mass range
$[10^{14}, 10^{16}]\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$.

```{python}
# Survey solid angle and integration limits
mf.set_area_sd(200.0)
mf.set_eval_limits(cosmo, np.log(1.0e14), np.log(1.0e16), 0.0, 2.0)
mf.prepare(cosmo)

# Comoving number density at z = 0.7
lnM_a = np.log(1.0e14) + np.log(1.0e2) * np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n)
dn_dlnM_a = np.array([mf.dn_dlnM(cosmo, lnM, 0.7) for lnM in lnM_a])

# NumCosmo takes masses as ln M; plot against log10(M), as the library's own
# log10MDelta parameters do
log10M_a = lnM_a / np.log(10.0)
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-hmf-massfunc
# | fig-cap: "Halo mass function $dn / d\\ln M$ at $z = 0.7$."
# | fig-width: 100%
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(log10M_a, dn_dlnM_a, "b", label="$z = 0.7$")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.xlabel(r"$\log_{10}(M / \mathrm{M}_\odot)$")
plt.ylabel(r"$dn / d\ln M$")
plt.title("Halo Mass Function")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.show()
```

Integrating over the mass range gives the number of halos per unit redshift, which we evaluate across
$z \in [0, 2]$ for the same $200\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ survey. The final argument requests an intermediary
spline for the mass integration, which is the faster choice when evaluating many redshifts in sequence.

```{python}
dndz_a = np.array(
    [mf.dn_dz(cosmo, np.log(1.0e14), np.log(1.0e16), z, True) for z in z_a]
)

# Redshift at which the counts peak
print(f"# peak at z = {z_a[np.argmax(dndz_a)]: .2f}")
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-hmf-dndz
# | fig-cap: >
# |   Number of halos per unit redshift for $M \in [10^{14},
# |   10^{16}]\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ over a $200\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ survey.
# | fig-width: 100%
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(
    z_a,
    dndz_a,
    "b",
    label=r"$M \in [10^{14}, 10^{16}], \; A = 200 \; \mathrm{deg}^2$",
)
plt.xlabel(r"$z$")
plt.ylabel(r"$dN/dz$")
plt.title("Number of Halos per Redshift")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.show()
```

The counts peak where comoving volume and the abundance of massive halos
balance.

## Conclusion

The example combines linear growth, the Eisenstein-Hu transfer function,
tophat-filtered variance, and the Tinker multiplicity function to compute
$dn/d\ln M$ and halo counts per redshift.
